lines.text: From a dot bouncing on a lab oscilloscope to worlds shared by millions, here are the consoles and the games that shaped video games.
It began in 1958 at Brookhaven lab, where a tennis match on an oscilloscope screen delighted visitors. It was one of the first games made just for fun.
Four years later, students at MIT wrote Spacewar, a duel of two rocket ships around a star, and it spread from lab to lab.
In 1972 the Magnavox Odyssey brought games home for the first time. It drew a few dots, so players taped plastic overlays to the screen.
That same year Atari's Pong, two paddles and a square ball, became the first hit video game and started the arcade business.
Then the Atari 2600 made swappable cartridges popular, and put video games into millions of living rooms for fifteen years.
From Japan came Space Invaders, rows of descending aliens and one lonely cannon. It turned games into a worldwide business.
Mattel answered with Intellivision, sharper graphics and real sports leagues, and adverts that mocked the Atari.
In 1980 a yellow circle chased by four ghosts won over all kinds of players. Pac-Man had no guns, and everyone knew his face.
Nintendo's Donkey Kong sent a carpenter up the scaffolding against a giant ape. That carpenter would soon be known as Mario.
ColecoVision came close to arcade quality at home, and shipped with Donkey Kong in the box.
But the boom went bust. In 1983 too many consoles and too many poor games drove buyers away, and the American market collapsed.
Nintendo brought it back with the Famicom, sold in the West as the Nintendo Entertainment System.
In Moscow, a programmer designed Tetris, falling blocks to fit into lines, a puzzle that would soon conquer the world.
Super Mario Bros. sent Mario running and jumping through eight worlds to save a princess, and became one of the best-selling games of its time.
The Legend of Zelda gave players a wide map to explore, and one of the first cartridges that could save your progress.
Sega struck back with the Genesis, called the Mega Drive outside North America, and the console war began.
Nintendo's Game Boy had a grey-green screen, but it was cheap, its batteries lasted, and it came with Tetris. It was everywhere.
The Super Nintendo joined the fight, sixteen bits against sixteen bits, for the living rooms of the early nineties.
In the arcades, Street Fighter Two packed the cabinets and set the pattern for fighting games ever since.
Sega found its mascot in Sonic, a blue hedgehog racing through loops at full speed, made to outrun Mario.
Nintendo took Mario racing in Super Mario Kart, the start of one of the best-selling racing series ever.
Newcomers tried to join in. The 3DO played games on CD, but its high price kept buyers away.
Atari's Jaguar promised sixty-four bits, but it was hard to program and had few good games. It was Atari's last home console.
On the PC, Doom arrived: fast, frightening, playable over a network, and given away in part for free. Millions played it.
Sega's Saturn did well in Japan, but it was costly and hard to program, and in the West it lost to a new rival.
That rival was Sony's PlayStation, born after a deal with Nintendo fell apart. Games on CD, aimed at adults too, made Sony the leader.
Nintendo stumbled with the Virtual Boy, red and black 3D through a visor. It was uncomfortable, and gone within a year.
Then came Pokemon Red and Blue on the Game Boy: catch creatures, train them, trade them with friends, and a vast franchise was born.
The Nintendo 64 brought 3D worlds home, and its analogue stick became part of every controller that followed.
Super Mario 64 showed everyone how to do it, with a camera the player could turn in a fully three-dimensional world.
Final Fantasy Seven, with its long story and film-like scenes, introduced Western players to the Japanese role-playing game.
StarCraft pitted three factions across space, became a national pastime in South Korea, and helped give birth to esports.
Half-Life told its story as you walked, without breaking for cut scenes, and set Valve on its rise.
Sega's Dreamcast had a modem for online play built in, ahead of its time. But it could not survive what came next, and Sega left consoles for good.
Fans turned Half-Life into Counter-Strike, rounds of bomb planting and hostage rescue that grew into a major esport.
What came next was the PlayStation 2, which played DVDs too and became one of the best-selling consoles ever made.
The Sims let players run the daily lives of little virtual people, and became one of the best-selling series on PC.
The Game Boy Advance brought a wide colour screen, and still played the old Game Boy games.
Nintendo's GameCube, a small cube with a handle, was loved for its games but outsold by the PlayStation 2.
Grand Theft Auto Three opened up a whole 3D city to roam, setting the model for open-world games, and stirring controversy along the way.
Halo made the first Xbox a success, and showed how a shooter should feel on a controller.
Microsoft had entered the race with the Xbox, built like a PC, and with Xbox Live it made online play on a console normal.
Valve launched Steam to update its own games. It grew into the main store where PC games are bought and played.
The first Call of Duty arrived, the start of one of the best-selling game series of all time.
Nintendo's DS folded open on two screens, one you could touch, and sold well over a hundred million.
World of Warcraft put thousands of players in one shared world. At its peak, well over ten million paid to play.
Sony's PlayStation Portable played games, music and films on small discs, but phones and the DS outsold it.
The Xbox 360 made online play, downloaded games and films part of an ordinary console.
On Roblox, players, many of them children, began building and sharing games of their own.
The PlayStation 3 started slowly at a high price, then recovered, and helped Blu-ray win its format war.
Then Nintendo went another way. With the Wii you swung the controller like a racket, and people who had never played joined in.
Wii Sports came in the box, tennis and bowling for grandparents and children alike, and sold tens of millions.
One programmer began Minecraft, a world of cubes to mine and build in. It became one of the best-selling games ever.
On phones, Angry Birds flung birds at pigs, and became one of the first mobile games to turn into a worldwide brand.
League of Legends, two teams of five, grew into one of the most played games on Earth and the biggest in esports.
On Twitch, people watched others play, live, with a chat running alongside. Amazon bought it in 2014.
The International, Dota 2's world championship, drew crowd-funded prize pools larger than any in esports.
Skyrim offered a whole fantasy land to wander. It sold tens of millions, and fans still play and mod it.
Candy Crush Saga had players swapping sweets across hundreds of levels, and showed how small purchases could earn a fortune.
The Wii U added a touch screen to the controller, but its name confused buyers and it sold poorly.
Valve's Dota 2 became one of the most played games on Steam, with the largest prizes in esports.
Grand Theft Auto Five gave players three lives to switch between, and its online mode kept it selling for more than a decade.
The PlayStation 4 sold well over a hundred million, far ahead of its rival.
That rival, the Xbox One, was pitched as a living-room box, and its high price and early policies cost it dearly.
The Oculus Rift, born from crowd funding and bought by Facebook, brought virtual reality into gamers' homes.
Pokemon Go sent players walking through real streets to catch creatures on their phones, downloaded many millions of times in weeks.
The Nintendo Switch was a handheld and a home console in one, and became one of Nintendo's biggest hits.
Breath of the Wild let players climb, glide and explore at will, often named among the best games ever made.
PUBG made battle royale a craze: a hundred players drop in, and one is left standing.
Fortnite took that idea, added building and made it free, earning from outfits and hosting concerts on its island.
Among Us, crewmates hunting a hidden impostor, became a global hit during the pandemic.
Rockstar's Red Dead Redemption Two, a Wild West epic, was one of the most praised games of its decade.
From China, Genshin Impact offered a free open world on phones, PCs and consoles, and became one of the highest-earning mobile games.
In 2020 Microsoft launched its fourth generation of Xbox, the same week as its old rival.
The PlayStation 5 brought a fast solid-state drive and a controller you could feel, and sold well despite shortages.
Elden Ring, hard and vast, its world written with George R. R. Martin, sold over twenty-five million copies.
In 2025 the Switch 2 arrived, with a bigger screen and magnetic controllers, and sold faster than any Nintendo console before it.
And now, Grand Theft Auto Six, set in a version of Florida, one of the most anticipated games ever made.
From a dot on an oscilloscope to whole worlds, and the next game is always just around the corner.
